posts.title: A letter from the editor, autumn
posts.excerpt: Why this issue is about rooms, and why we asked ten writers to describe the one they read in.
posts.content:
Every issue begins in a borrowed room. This one began in the reading room of the old ward library, ten minutes before closing, when the lamps go off one table at a time.

We asked ten writers to describe the room they read in. Five wrote essays and five wrote poems; none of them described the same kind of room, and all of them mentioned the light.

Read slowly. Keep your place with the ribbon. — Michiko Asahina

posts.title: Notes on a poem draft
posts.excerpt: Seven versions of a six-line poem, and the one word that changed everything.
posts.content:
Sora Nakaya’s “Paper Moon, Kitchen Window” reached us as a twenty-line poem. It is six lines in the issue.

The drafts went back and forth by post four times. Most of the cutting was his; the one word we asked for was “still”, and he kept it.

posts.title: In praise of reading rooms
posts.excerpt: Tall shelves, two chairs by a window and the particular quiet of a room kept for reading.
posts.content:
A reading room is the only public place where silence is shared on purpose. Nobody is waiting for you there, and nobody minds how slowly you turn the page.

The small reading room of the ward library on Kawasemi-zaka has tall pale shelves, one table and two chairs by the window. We have held three readings there, and each time the room did half the work.

posts.title: How an issue is sewn
posts.excerpt: Folded sheets, a waxed thread and a ribbon tipped in by hand: two days at the printer two streets away.
posts.content:
Each issue is printed in five folded sections of sixteen pages. The printer sews them together with a waxed thread, then trims three edges and leaves the fourth soft.

The ribbon is tipped in by hand before the cover goes on. It takes two people two days for 1,800 copies.

posts.title: Why we still number the pages
posts.excerpt: On folios, contents pages and the small pleasure of turning to page sixty-two.
posts.content:
The number at the foot of a page is called a folio. A contents page is only a promise until the folios keep it.

We set ours small, in a mono face, at the outer corner. Readers tell us they use them to arrange to meet: “see you on page sixty-two”.

posts.title: Dispatch day, on foot
posts.excerpt: Six hundred sleeves, two hand carts and the walk down Kawasemi-zaka to the post office.
posts.content:
Four times a year the office smells of glue and brown paper. We fold the sleeves on the long table and stack them by postcode.

Then two hand carts down the hill to the post office, which knows us by now and opens a second counter.
